svg.title: Removing the bladder or keeping it: the shape of the evidence on both roads, the three directions of selection bias, and salvage cystectomy
svg.desc: Schematic putting the two roads in muscle-invasive bladder cancer - radical cystectomy and trimodality therapy (resection plus concurrent chemoradiotherapy) - on one table, with every cell carrying its study design, population, follow-up and number of patients. The top of the figure states that there is no successfully completed randomised trial on this question, quoting the EAU 2026 guideline verbatim: "No successfully completed RCTs are available comparing the outcomes of TMT with RC." Two cards follow. SPARE was a randomised feasibility study: first patient 20 July 2007, accrual closed 12 February 2010 on the advice of the independent data monitoring committee and the trial steering committee, with only 45 patients in all; of 796 screened patients with T2-T3 N0M0 disease 490 were ineligible, 165 were approached and 45 consented (27%), and of the 120 who declined, 51 preferred radiotherapy and 25 preferred surgery. The second card is DAVECA 8201 from 1991: a randomised trial, 183 patients, T2 to T4a, recruited 1983 to 1986, but it compared preoperative radiotherapy of 40 Gy plus planned cystectomy against radical radiotherapy of 60 Gy with cystectomy only for residual tumour, without concurrent chemotherapy - so it is not the trimodality therapy meant today. The second panel is Zlotta 2023: retrospective, propensity score matched and inverse-probability weighted, not a randomised trial; clinical T2-T4 N0M0 disease, 2005 to 2017, 722 patients (440 cystectomy, 282 trimodality therapy), median follow-up 4.4 and 4.9 years. The entry criteria are boxed separately: a solitary tumour under 7 cm, no hydronephrosis or unilateral only, no extensive or multifocal carcinoma in situ; and those 440 cystectomy patients were only 29% of all radical cystectomies done over the same period. The matched results are set side by side: five-year metastasis-free survival 74% against 74%, five-year cancer-specific survival 83% against 85% (p=0.057), five-year disease-free survival 76% against 76%; underneath, the figure states that this can only be read as "in this selected group of patients, these endpoints could not be told apart", and that not being able to tell them apart is not the same as being equally good. The third panel sets out what each road carries. For radical cystectomy: the EAU gives a strong recommendation in T2-T4a N0M0 disease, and on this operation alone about half of patients live beyond five years; 90-day mortality varies with the cohort - 2.5% in a selected university-centre cohort, 4.7% pooled across 66 retrospective studies, 5.6% in the Dutch national registry of 9,287 patients, and in the randomised SWOG S1011 trial 7% (19/292) in the extended lymph node dissection arm against 2% (7/300) in the standard arm; 90-day complications pooled 58.5% (36.1% to 80.5%); and people who have surgery get a pathological stage, of those 440, 44% pT3-4 and 26% node positive. For trimodality therapy: radiotherapy is 64 Gy in 32 fractions over six and a half weeks or 55 Gy in 20 fractions over four weeks with concurrent radiosensitising chemotherapy; in the randomised phase II RTOG 0712 trial treatment-related grade 3-4 toxicity was 21/33 (64%) in one arm and 18/33 (55%) in the other, and the meta-analysis of matched cohorts pooled acute grade 3 or worse toxicity at 11.4%; salvage cystectomy pooled across 73 studies and 9,110 patients followed beyond five years runs at about 19.2%, roughly one person in five, with an EAU modern-series range of 10% to 30% and a complication rate for that operation of 67% to 72%; none of the three guidelines gives a stopping point for cystoscopy after treatment, and quoting BC2001 patient-reported data the EAU records that about one third still score bladder symptoms below baseline at five years; people who keep the bladder only ever have a clinical stage. The fourth panel draws selection bias as three arrows, with "makes trimodality therapy look better" at the left end and "makes radical cystectomy look better" at the right. The first arrow points left: a meta-analysis restricted to matched cohort studies, 87 studies and 28,218 patients, overall survival hazard ratio 1.05 (95% confidence interval 0.78-1.40) and cancer-specific survival 1.05 (0.69-1.58), no difference detectable, the bias being that trimodality patients in single-centre and matched cohorts are selected, motivated and have favourable tumours, while the authors still call for evidence from high-quality controlled trials. The second arrow points right: NCDB 2004 to 2013, AJCC stage II to III, 32,300 patients, hazard ratio for death after matching 1.406 (1.235-1.601); SEER 2010 to 2022, T2N0M0, 10,495 patients, five-year overall survival after matching 62.6% with cystectomy against 36.7% with trimodality therapy; the bias sits in fields a registry cannot see - the international multicentre RISC cohort measured it, and people taking the preservation road were older, had worse performance status and more comorbidity, all three with p below 0.01. The third arrow also points right: Robesti 2025 reconstructed the survival curves of 6 studies and 8,594 patients and found that 10 of 12 reported endpoints carried an imbalance in dropping out of follow-up (informative censoring), overall favouring cystectomy, and that after correction cystectomy was still superior, with five-year overall survival 42% against 30%. The figure notes that this cell cuts against the claim that too little bladder preservation is being done, which is why it has to be shown. The fifth panel is quality of life: a cross-sectional retrospective study at two hospitals, 226 people suitable for either road and disease-free for at least two years, response rate 77%, 173 replies (64 trimodality therapy, 109 cystectomy), median follow-up 5.6 years; after propensity score adjustment the trimodality group scored 9.7 points higher on global quality of life (out of 100, p=0.001), 8.7 to 32.1 points higher on sexual function and 14.8 points higher on body image, with similar urinary symptom scores; the authors themselves conclude that long-term quality of life is good on both roads and that whether trimodality therapy is better needs prospective study, and the two groups were two years apart between diagnosis and questionnaire. The last panel lists three readings that are not allowed - "bladder preservation is the second-best option", "bladder preservation is just as good", "no operation means an easier time" - each with its reason; discloses that the person who drew the figure does the radiotherapy half of trimodality therapy himself, and that the third arrow and the salvage cystectomy cell have not been made smaller; and closes with the EAU line "For all suitable candidates, both bladder-preserving techniques and RC should be discussed" and NICE NG2 1.5.5 "Offer a choice of radical cystectomy or radiotherapy with a radiosensitiser", stating that what the figure gives is questions to ask your doctors, not an answer.

g.text: MUSCLE-INVASIVE BLADDER CANCER - TWO ROADS, AND WHAT THE EVIDENCE ACTUALLY IS
Two roads on one table: the design, population, follow-up
The two roads in muscle-invasive bladder cancer - radical cystectomy, or resection followed by concurrent chemoradiotherapy, that is,
trimodality therapy. This figure does not tell you which road to take. It does one thing: it puts the design, the population, the follow-up, the
number of patients, and whether the trimodality patients were a selected group, next to each figure quoted.
The cohorts, designs and endpoints of the underlying studies differ, so the data points must not be compared directly.
There is no successfully completed randomised trial on this question. What can be cited today are matched cohorts and registry data - they do not point the
same way, and all three directions of bias have to be read together.
First thing: there is no successfully completed randomised trial
No successfully completed RCTs are available comparing the outcomes of TMT with RC.
The EAU 2026 guideline's own sentence: comparing trimodality therapy with radical cystectomy, there is no successfully completed randomised trial.
The one that closed for insufficient accrual
first patient 20 July 2007; accrual closed 12 February 2010 on the advice of the
independent data monitoring committee and the trial steering committee
of 796 screened patients with T2-T3 N0M0 disease, 490 were ineligible; 165 were
approached and 45 consented (27%); of the 120 who declined, 51 preferred
The authors' own conclusion: patients and clinicians both held strong preferences
and were unwilling to let a randomisation decide the road, and clinicians never
shared a consensus that the two roads are equivalent.
The randomised trial from 1991 was not comparing this
183 patients, T2 to T4a, recruited 1983 to 1986
"preoperative radiotherapy 40 Gy plus planned cystectomy" against "radical
radiotherapy 60 Gy with cystectomy only for residual tumour"
no concurrent chemotherapy - that is not the trimodality therapy meant today
So it cannot stand as randomised evidence for the two roads as they are now.
The highest-grade comparison available compares a selected group of people
Zlotta 2023: a retrospective analysis from three North American university centres using propensity score matching with inverse probability weighting.
Propensity score matching lines the two groups up on recorded fields such as age, stage and hydronephrosis before comparing them; it holds down the
differences you can see, not the ones nobody recorded. It is not a randomised trial.
retrospective, propensity score matched and inverse-probability weighted (not
clinical T2-T4 N0M0 urothelial carcinoma, 2005 to 2017
The entry criteria are the point, and belong with the figures every time they are quoted
no extensive or multifocal carcinoma in situ
That is, people for whom both roads were open on tumour grounds. Those 440 cystectomy patients were only 29% of all radical cystectomies done at those centres over
the same period - of every ten people who had the bladder removed, only about three had both roads open on tumour grounds in the first place.
This can only be written as "in this selected group of patients, these endpoints could not be told apart". Not being able to tell them apart is not the same as being equally
good - the selected population, the retrospective design and the four-to-five-year follow-up each limit how hard the sentence can be put.

The authors' own conclusion: long-term quality of life is good on both roads, and whether trimodality therapy is better needs prospective study to confirm. The two groups
were also two years apart between diagnosis and filling in the questionnaire - this can only be treated as a clue.
Three readings this figure must not be given

The person who drew this figure has an interest in it: the radiotherapy half of trimodality therapy is what he does himself, and this topic argues that too little
bladder preservation is done in Taiwan. So the third arrow - the one that cuts against that argument - is drawn the same size as the other two, and the salvage
cystectomy cell has not been made smaller.
The guidelines themselves put "both roads must be discussed" in writing. EAU: "For all suitable candidates, both bladder-preserving techniques and RC should be
discussed". NICE NG2, 1.5.5: "Offer a choice of radical cystectomy or radiotherapy with a radiosensitiser". What this figure gives you is questions to ask your doctors,
Schematic, redrawn from the EAU guidelines on muscle-invasive and metastatic bladder cancer (2026 edition), Zlotta 2023, SPARE (Huddart 2017), Sell 1991, Matsukawa 2025,
Cahn 2017, He 2026, Rose 2016, Robesti 2025, Schuettfort 2021, RTOG 0712 (Coen 2019), Maibom 2021, Richters 2021, SWOG S1011 (Lerner 2024), Mak 2016 and NICE NG2; not
reproduced from their figures. The cohorts, designs and endpoints of the underlying studies differ, so the data points must not be compared directly.
